'''Hamilton Heights''' is a neighborhood in the [[Upper Manhattan|northern part]] of [[Manhattan]] in [[New York City]].  It is the northernmost part of the [[West Harlem, Manhattan|West Harlem]] area, along with [[Manhattanville, Manhattan|Manhattanville]] and [[Morningside Heights, Manhattan|Morningside Heights]] to its south,<ref>{{cite web|url = http://www.cb9m.org/district | access-date = March 31, 2020 | title = The District - Manhattan Community Board 9 | website = www.cb9m.org}}</ref> and it contains the sub-neighborhood and historic district of [[Sugar Hill, Manhattan|Sugar Hill]].<ref>{{Cite book |last=James |first=Davida Siwisa |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=SQ73EAAAQBAJ |title=Hamilton Heights and Sugar Hill: Alexander Hamilton's Old Harlem Neighborhood Through the Centuries |date=2024 |publisher=Fordham University Press |isbn=978-1-5315-0614-8 |edition=1st |location=New York}}</ref> [[Washington Heights, Manhattan|Washington Heights]] lies to Hamilton Heights' north, and to its east is [[Harlem|Central Harlem]].<ref name="Citycyclopedia">{{cite enc-nyc|pages=519-520}}</ref>

Hamilton Heights is bounded by 135th Street to the south, [[Riverside Drive (Manhattan)|Riverside Drive]] to the west, [[155th Street (Manhattan)|155th Street]] to the north, and Edgecombe Avenue and [[St. Nicholas Avenue|Saint Nicholas Avenue]] to the east. The community derives its name from Founding Father [[Alexander Hamilton]], who lived the last two years of his life in what is now the [[Hamilton Grange National Memorial]], back when [[Upper Manhattan]] was mostly farmland.<ref name="Citycyclopedia"/>

Hamilton Heights is part of [[Manhattan Community Board 9|Manhattan Community District 9]], and its primary [[ZIP Code]]s are 10031, 10032, and 10039.<ref name="NYCPlanning"/> It is patrolled by the 30th Precinct of the [[New York City Police Department]].

==Demographics==
Based on data from the [[2010 United States census]], the population of Hamilton Heights was 48,520, a decrease of 2,035 (4.0%) from the 50,555 counted in [[2000 United States census|2000]]. Covering an area of {{convert|367.41|acres}}, the neighborhood had a population density of {{convert|132.1|PD/acre|PD/sqmi PD/sqkm}}.<ref name=PLP5>[http://www1.nyc.gov/assets/planning/download/pdf/data-maps/nyc-population/census2010/t_pl_p5_nta.pdf Table PL-P5 NTA: Total Population and Persons Per Acre - New York City Neighborhood Tabulation Areas*, 2010], Population Division - [[New York City]] Department of City Planning, February 2012. Accessed June 16, 2016.</ref> The racial makeup of the neighborhood was 10.9% (5,287) [[White (U.S. Census)|White]], 32.2% (15,646) [[African American (U.S. Census)|African American]], 0.2% (119) [[Native American (U.S. Census)|Native American]], 2.2% (1,067) [[Asian (U.S. Census)|Asian]], 0.0% (15) [[Pacific Islander (U.S. Census)|Pacific Islander]], 0.4% (178) from [[Race (United States Census)|other races]], and 1.8% (884) from two or more races. [[Hispanic (U.S. Census)|Hispanic]] or [[Latino (U.S. Census)|Latino]] of any race were 52.2% (25,324) of the population.<ref name=PLP3A>[http://www1.nyc.gov/assets/planning/download/pdf/data-maps/nyc-population/census2010/t_pl_p3a_nta.pdf Table PL-P3A NTA: Total Population by Mutually Exclusive Race and Hispanic Origin - New York City Neighborhood Tabulation Areas*, 2010], Population Division - [[New York City]] Department of City Planning, March 29, 2011. Accessed June 14, 2016.</ref>

The most significant changes in the racial composition of Hamilton Heights from 2000 to 2010 were the increase in the White population by 231% (3,691) and the decrease in the Black population by 26% (5,366). The Hispanic / Latino population also decreased by 2% (648) but remained the majority. Meanwhile, the Asian population increased by 90% (506) but remained a small minority, and the small population of all other races decreased by 15% (218).<ref>{{cite web | url = http://www.urbanresearchmaps.org/plurality/files/RaceEthnic%20Change%20by%20Neighborhood%205-23-11.xls | title = Race / Ethnic Change by Neighborhood | publisher = Center for Urban Research, The Graduate Center, CUNY | date = May 23, 2011 | access-date = March 20, 2020 |format=Excel file}}</ref>

The entirety of Community District 9, which consists of Hamilton Heights, [[Manhattanville, Manhattan|Manhattanville]], and [[Morningside Heights, Manhattan|Morningside Heights]], had 111,287 inhabitants as of [[New York City Department of Health and Mental Hygiene|NYC Health]]'s 2018 Community Health Profile, with an average life expectancy of 81.4 years.<ref name="CHP2018">{{Cite web|url=https://www1.nyc.gov/assets/doh/downloads/pdf/data/2018chp-mn9.pdf|title=Morningside Heights and Hamilton Heights (Including Hamilton Heights, Manhattanville, Morningside Heights and West Harlem)|date=2018|website=nyc.gov|publisher=NYC Health|access-date=March 2, 2019}}</ref>{{Rp|2, 20}} This is about the same as the median life expectancy of 81.2 for all New York City neighborhoods.<ref name=":21">{{Cite web|url=https://www1.nyc.gov/assets/doh/downloads/pdf/tcny/community-health-assessment-plan.pdf|title=2016-2018 Community Health Assessment and Community Health Improvement Plan: Take Care New York 2020|date=2016|website=[[government of New York City|nyc.gov]]|publisher=[[New York City Department of Health and Mental Hygiene]]|access-date=September 8, 2017|archive-date=September 9, 2017|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170909004755/https://www1.nyc.gov/assets/doh/downloads/pdf/tcny/community-health-assessment-plan.pdf|url-status=dead}}</ref>{{Rp|53 (PDF p. 84)}} Most residents are children and middle-aged adults: 34% are between the ages of 25–44, while 21% are between 45 and 64, and 17% are between 0–17. The ratio of college-aged and elderly residents was lower, at 16% and 12% respectively.<ref name="CHP2018" />{{Rp|2}}

{{As of|2017|post=,}} the median [[household income]] in Community District 9 was $50,048,<ref name="CB9PUMA">{{cite web|url=https://censusreporter.org/profiles/79500US3603802-nyc-manhattan-community-district-9-hamilton-heights-manhattanville-west-harlem-puma-ny/|title=NYC-Manhattan Community District 9--Hamilton Heights, Manhattanville & West Harlem PUMA, NY|access-date=July 17, 2018|archive-date=March 26, 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190326154923/https://censusreporter.org/profiles/79500US3603802-nyc-manhattan-community-district-9-hamilton-heights-manhattanville-west-harlem-puma-ny/|url-status=dead}}</ref> though the median income in Hamilton Heights individually was $43,673.<ref name="stats"/> In 2018, an estimated 24% of Community District 9 residents lived in [[poverty]], compared to 14% in all of Manhattan and 20% in all of New York City. One in twelve residents (8%) were [[unemployment|unemployed]], compared to 7% in Manhattan and 9% in New York City. Rent burden, or the percentage of residents who had difficulty paying their rent, was 51% in Community District 9, compared to the boroughwide and citywide rates of 45% and 51% respectively. Based on this calculation, {{as of|2018|lc=y}}, Community District 9 was considered to be [[gentrification|gentrifying]]: according to the Community Health Profile, the district was low-income in 1990 and saw above-median rent growth up to 2010.<ref name="CHP2018" />{{Rp|7}}

== Housing and diversity ==
{{multiple image
|align=center
|direction=horizontal
|total_width=600
|image1=Hamilton Heights.jpg
|caption1=Convent Avenue in Hamilton Heights
|image2=Francis F. Palmer House (51624552539).jpg
|caption2=The Holy Fathers Russian Orthodox Church [[Russian Orthodox Church Outside Russia]]
}}
Most of the housing dates from the extension of the elevated and subway lines at the end of the 19th and the start of the 20th century.<ref name="Citycyclopedia"/> This fairly elegant housing became less desirable to white residents in the 1930s and 1940s as the population changed from white to black, even though the black residents were just as affluent as the white residents.<ref name="Citycyclopedia"/> There are spacious apartment buildings, [[brownstone]]s, and other [[Terraced house|row houses]] prominently lining the leafy eastern streets of Hamilton Heights, an area traditionally home to a substantial black professional class. The brownstone revival of the 1960s and 1970s led to a new movement of middle-class blacks in the area. [[Hispanic and Latino Americans|Hispanics]] arrived in large numbers in the 1980s, with [[Dominican Americans#New York City|Dominicans]] making up the majority.<ref name="Citycyclopedia"/> Today the local population is changing again, with Hispanics constituting a majority of the population followed by [[African American]]s, [[West Indian Americans|West Indians]], and [[White Americans|Whites]]. [[Gentrification]] since 2005 has dramatically increased the proportion of non-Hispanic whites. Many actors, artists, teachers, and other professionals now reside in Hamilton Heights.<ref name="nyt">{{cite web |title=Hamilton Heights: Awaiting a Bounce (Published 2011) |website=[[The New York Times]] |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20111211203515/https://www.nytimes.com/2011/06/12/realestate/hamilton-heights-awaiting-a-bounce.html?pagewanted=all |archive-date=2011-12-11 |url-status=live |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2011/06/12/realestate/hamilton-heights-awaiting-a-bounce.html?pagewanted=all&_r=0}}</ref>

After the [[Russian Revolution]], especially after the 1940s, many [[Ukrainians]], Russian [[White émigré]], and [[Polish people|Polish]] found their way to New York City. Hamilton Heights had a very heavy population of [[Eastern European]] heritage, with a predominantly large number of [[Russians]] living in this immediate area. There were a couple of [[Russian Orthodox]] Churches erected, Russian book stores, bakeries, grocery and delicatessen stores, and theatres all along [[Broadway (Manhattan)|Broadway]]. The house on the corner of Broadway and W. 141st Street was known as the "Russian House" (Русский Дом), and a Russian library was on the other corner. During the late 1950s and throughout the 1960s, a lot of these Russians began to move out to suburban areas of New York and [[New Jersey]]. The only remaining landmark of this era is the Holy Fathers Russian Orthodox Church [[Russian Orthodox Church Outside Russia]], located on 524 W. 153rd Street,<ref>[http://www.russianorthodoxchurch.ws/01newstucture/pagesen/english/pages/news/oldestchurch.html "The Parish of the Holy Fathers Church"] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20111210021705/http://www.russianorthodoxchurch.ws/01newstucture/pagesen/english/pages/news/oldestchurch.html |date=December 10, 2011 }}</ref> with some notable [[Russian Americans]] buried at the bordering Trinity Cemetery.<ref name="nyt"/>

==Notable sites==
[[Image:North River Wastewater Plant 2007 jeh.jpg|thumb|center|upright=3.5|{{center|Hamilton Heights, as seen from the [[Hudson River]]}}]]
Hamilton Heights is the home of [[City College of New York]] (CCNY), [[Dance Theatre of Harlem]], [[The Harlem School of the Arts]], and [[Aaron Davis Hall]].
[[File:Benziger1.jpg|alt=large brick house at night, with large tree out front and iron fence surrounding property|thumb|Image of the Benziger House at night, Spring 2026]]
Nearly all of Hamilton Heights is on a district listed on the [[National Register of Historic Places]].<ref name="Cultural Resource Information System"/> Historic Hamilton Heights comprises the [[Hamilton Heights Historic District]] and the Hamilton Heights/[[Sugar Hill, Manhattan|Sugar Hill]] Historic District Extension, both designated by the [[New York City Landmarks Preservation Commission]] and listed on the NRHP.<ref name="Experience NYCLPC">{{cite web | title=Experience | website=Experience Builder System | url=https://experience.arcgis.com/experience/fa1bcaad31374a88839da3f0166e640a/page/Page#data_s=id%3AdataSource_1-LPC_HistoricBuildings_Service_768%3A34682%2Cid%3AdataSource_1-197a7cf710c-layer-13%3A37715 | access-date=2026-06-17}}</ref><ref name="Cultural Resource Information System">{{cite web |title=Cultural Resource Information System (CRIS) |publisher=[[New York State Office of Parks, Recreation and Historic Preservation]] |date=November 7, 2014 |url=https://cris.parks.ny.gov/ |access-date=July 20, 2023 |archive-date=April 4, 2019 |archive-url=http://webarchive.loc.gov/all/20190404141934/https://cris.parks.ny.gov/ |url-status=live }}</ref> The '''West Harlem Historic District''', comprising the area west of Broadway from 135th to 153rd Streets, is also on the NRHP.<ref name="Cultural Resource Information System"/> Prominent historic buildings in the neighborhood include the Nicholas C. And Agnes Benziger House at the corner of Edgecomb Avenue and 150th St.<ref>{{Cite web |date=November 6, 2021 |title=The Historic Nicholas C. And Agnes Benziger House In Hamilton Heights In Harlem |url=https://www.harlemworldmagazine.com/the-historic-nicholas-c-and-agnes-benziger-house-in-hamilton-heights-in-harlem/ |access-date=October 20, 2026 |website=Harlem World}}</ref>

[[File:Shepard Hall.JPG|thumb|right|Shepard Hall, on the [[City College of New York]]'s [[North Campus (City College of New York)|North Campus]]]]

One of the highest hills in Hamilton Heights slopes up from the [[Hudson River]] at [[155th Street (Manhattan)|155th Street]], and contains the Trinity Cemetery.<ref name="Citycyclopedia" /> Many individual buildings in the district are also landmarked, including the [[North Campus (City College of New York)|North Campus]] of CCNY, the building that once housed the [[High School of Music & Art]], and the former [[32nd Police Precinct Station]].<ref name="Experience NYCLPC" />


The [[Audubon Mural Project]] paints the neighborhood with images of the birds depicted by [[John James Audubon]] in his early 19th century folio [[The Birds of America]].<ref name="DelsonAnew">{{cite news|last1=Delson|first1=Susan|title=Retracing Audubon's Steps, Painting His Birds Anew|url=https://www.wsj.com/articles/retracing-audubons-steps-painting-his-birds-anew-1445539879|access-date=October 26, 2017|publisher=Wall Street Journal|date=October 23, 2015}}</ref>



===Parks===
[[File:Carmansville Playground eq 2021 jeh.jpg|thumb|Carmansville Playground]]
The neighborhood offers several parks, including the [[Riverbank State Park]], embedded in [[Riverside Park (Manhattan)|Riverside Park]], which runs along the [[Hudson River]]  west of Hamilton Heights.<ref name="Planning, Power and Politics: A Case Study of the Land Use and Siting History of the North River Water Pollution Control Plant">{{cite journal|last1=Miller|first1=Vernice D.|url=http://ir.lawnet.fordham.edu/cgi/viewcontent.cgi?article=1405&context=ulj|journal=[[Fordham Urban Law Journal]]|date=1994|volume=21|issue=3|title=Planning, Power and Politics: A Case Study of the Land Use and Siting History of the North River Water Pollution Control Plant}}</ref> Other parks in the neighborhood include [[Jackie Robinson Park]],<ref>{{cite web | title=Jackie Robinson Park : NYC Parks | website=New York City Department of Parks & Recreation | date=June 26, 1939 | url=https://www.nycgovparks.org/parks/jackie-robinson-park_manhattan | access-date=March 24, 2020}}</ref> [[St. Nicholas Park]],<ref>{{cite web | title=St. Nicholas Park : NYC Parks | website=New York City Department of Parks & Recreation | date=June 26, 1939 | url=https://www.nycgovparks.org/parks/st-nicholas-park | access-date=March 24, 2020}}</ref> and smaller sites such as Johnny Hartman Square,<ref>{{cite web | title=Johnny Hartman Square : NYC Parks | website=New York City Department of Parks & Recreation | date=June 26, 1939 | url=https://www.nycgovparks.org/parks/johnny-hartman-square | access-date=March 24, 2020}}</ref> Carmansville Playground,<ref>{{cite web | title=Carmansville Playground : NYC Parks | website=New York City Department of Parks & Recreation | date=June 26, 1939 | url=https://www.nycgovparks.org/parks/carmansville-playground | access-date=March 24, 2020}}</ref> and [[William A. Harris Garden]].

==Police and crime==
Hamilton Heights is served mostly by the 30th Precinct of the [[New York City Police Department|NYPD]], located at 451 West 151st Street,<ref name="NYPD 30th Precinct">{{Cite web|url=https://www1.nyc.gov/site/nypd/bureaus/patrol/precincts/30th-precinct.page|title=NYPD – 30th Precinct|website=www.nyc.gov|publisher=[[New York City Police Department]]|access-date=October 3, 2016}}</ref> although the City College area south of 141st Street and east of [[Tenth Avenue (Manhattan)|Amsterdam Avenue]] is actually served by the 26th Precinct.<ref name="NYPD 26th Precinct">{{Cite web|url=https://www1.nyc.gov/site/nypd/bureaus/patrol/precincts/26th-precinct.page|title=NYPD – 26th Precinct|website=www.nyc.gov|publisher=[[New York City Police Department]]|access-date=October 3, 2016}}</ref> The 30th Precinct has a lower crime rate than in the 1990s, with crimes across all categories having decreased by 78.0% between 1990 and 2019. The precinct reported 4 murders, 20 rapes, 190 robberies, 178 felony assaults, 69 burglaries, 289 grand larcenies, and 27 grand larcenies auto in 2019.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www1.nyc.gov/assets/nypd/downloads/pdf/crime_statistics/cs-en-us-030pct.pdf|title=30th Precinct CompStat Report|website=www.nyc.gov|publisher=[[New York City Police Department]]|access-date=March 18, 2020}}</ref> Of the five major violent felonies (murder, rape, felony assault, robbery, and burglary), the 30th Precinct had a rate of 760 crimes per 100,000 residents in 2019, compared to the boroughwide average of 632 crimes per 100,000 and the citywide average of 572 crimes per 100,000.<ref name = "crime map"/><ref>{{cite web | url = https://www1.nyc.gov/assets/nypd/downloads/pdf/analysis_and_planning/historical-crime-data/seven-major-felony-offenses-2000-2019.pdf | title = Citywide Seven Major Felony Offenses 2000-2019 | publisher = [[New York Police Department]] | access-date = March 23, 2020 | website = www.nyc.gov}}</ref><ref>{{cite web | url = https://www1.nyc.gov/assets/nypd/downloads/pdf/analysis_and_planning/historical-crime-data/seven-major-felony-offenses-by-precinct-2000-2019.pdf | title = Citywide Seven Major Felony Offenses by Precinct 2000-2019 | publisher = [[New York Police Department]] | access-date = March 23, 2020 | website = www.nyc.gov}}</ref>

{{as of|2018}}, Manhattan Community District 9 has a non-fatal assault hospitalization rate of 57 per 100,000 people, compared to the boroughwide rate of 49 per 100,000 and the citywide rate of 59 per 100,000. Its incarceration rate is 633 per 100,000 people, compared to the boroughwide rate of 407 per 100,000 and the citywide rate of 425 per 100,000.<ref name="CHP2018" />{{Rp|8}}

In 2019, the highest concentrations of felony assaults in Hamilton Heights were near the intersection of 135th Street and [[Broadway (Manhattan)|Broadway]], where there were 10 felony assaults, and near the intersection of [[145th Street (Manhattan)|145th Street]] and [[Tenth Avenue (Manhattan)|Amsterdam Avenue]], where there were 11. The highest concentrations of robberies were nearby, around the intersection of 137th Street and Broadway, where there were 11 robberies, and around the intersection of 145th Street and Broadway, where there were 14.<ref name = "crime map">{{cite web | url = https://maps.nyc.gov/crime/ | access-date = March 23, 2020 | title = NYC Crime Map | website = www.nyc.gov | publisher = [[New York City Police Department]]}}</ref>

==Fire safety==
[[File:Engine 80 Ladder 23 503 W139 jeh.jpg|thumb|FDNY Engine 80 Ladder 23]]
Hamilton Heights is served by the [[New York City Fire Department]] (FDNY)'s Engine Company 80/Ladder Company 23, located at 503 West 139th Street.<ref>{{cite web | title=Engine Company 80/Ladder Company 24 | website=FDNYtrucks.com | url=http://www.fdnytrucks.com/files/html/manhattan/e80.htm | access-date=March 14, 2019}}</ref><ref>{{Cite FDNY locations}}</ref>

==Health==
[[Preterm birth|Preterm]] and [[teenage pregnancy|teenage]] births in Community District 9 are lower than the city average. In Community District 9, there were 82 preterm births per 1,000 [[live birth (human)|live births]] (compared to 87 per 1,000 citywide), and 10.9 births to teenage mothers per 1,000 live births (compared to 19.3 per 1,000 citywide).<ref name="CHP2018" />{{Rp|11}} Community District 9 has a low population of residents who are [[Health insurance coverage in the United States|uninsured]]. In 2018, this population was estimated to be 11%, slightly less than the citywide rate of 12%.<ref name="CHP2018" />{{Rp|14}}

The concentration of [[particulates|fine particulate matter]], the deadliest type of [[air pollution|air pollutant]], in Community District 9 is {{convert|0.008|mg/m3|oz/ft3}}, more than the city average.<ref name="CHP2018" />{{Rp|9}} Seventeen percent of Community District 9 residents are [[Smoking|smokers]], which is more than the city average of 14% of residents being smokers.<ref name="CHP2018" />{{Rp|13}} In Community District 9, 21% of residents are [[Obesity|obese]], 10% are [[Diabetes mellitus|diabetic]], and 29% have [[hypertension|high blood pressure]]—compared to the citywide averages of 24%, 11%, and 28% respectively.<ref name="CHP2018" />{{Rp|16}} In addition, 25% of children are obese, compared to the citywide average of 20%.<ref name="CHP2018" />{{Rp|12}}

Eighty-eight percent of residents eat some fruits and vegetables every day, which is about the same as the city's average of 87%. In 2018, 83% of residents described their health as "good", "very good", or "excellent", more than the city's average of 78%.<ref name="CHP2018" />{{Rp|13}} For every supermarket in Community District 9, there are 11 [[convenience store|bodegas]].<ref name="CHP2018" />{{Rp|10}}

The nearest hospital is the [[NYC Health + Hospitals/Harlem|Harlem Hospital Center]], located in [[Central Harlem]].<ref>{{cite web | title=Manhattan Hospital Listings | website=New York Hospitals | url=http://www.allny.com/health/hosp-manhattan.html | access-date=March 20, 2019}}</ref>

==Politics==
[[File:Rep. Adriano Espaillat 117th Official Photo.jpg|thumb|[[Adriano Espaillat]]]]
Politically, Hamilton Heights is in [[New York's 13th congressional district]] for the U.S. House of Representatives, represented by [[Democratic Party (United States)|Democrat]] [[Adriano Espaillat]] since 2017.<ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.nytimes.com/interactive/2018/11/06/us/elections/results-house-elections.html|title=U.S. House Election Results 2018|date=January 28, 2019|newspaper=[[The New York Times]]|access-date=February 21, 2019}}</ref> On the state level, it is in the [[New York State Senate]]'s  [[New York's 30th State Senate district|30th district]], represented by Democrat [[Cordell Cleare]], and the [[New York State Assembly]]'s 71st and 72nd districts represented by Democrats [[Al Taylor (politician)|Al Taylor]] and [[Manny De Los Santos]], respectively.<ref>[http://www.latfor.state.ny.us/maps/2012a/AD_map_rep_068.pdf Assembly District 68] {{Webarchive |url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190803211659/https://www.latfor.state.ny.us/maps/2012a/AD_map_rep_068.pdf |date=August 3, 2019 }}, New York State Legislative Task Force on Demographic Research and Reapportionment. Accessed May 5, 2017.</ref><ref>[http://www.latfor.state.ny.us/maps/2012s/SD_nyc.pdf 2012 Senate District Maps: New York City] {{Webarchive |url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210224202014/https://www.latfor.state.ny.us/maps/2012s/SD_nyc.pdf |date=February 24, 2021}}, New York State Legislative Task Force on Demographic Research and Reapportionment. ==Post offices and ZIP Codes==
Hamilton Heights is located in multiple [[ZIP Code]]s. Most of the neighborhood is in 10031; however, the area north of 153rd Street is in 10032, and the [[Polo Grounds Towers]] are in 10039.<ref>{{cite web | title=Hamilton Heights, New York City-Manhattan, New York Zip Code Boundary Map (NY) | website=United States Zip Code Boundary Map (USA) | url=https://www.zipmap.net/New_York/New_York_County/Z_Hamilton_Heights.htm | access-date=March 26, 2019}}</ref>  The [[United States Postal Service]] operates two post offices in or near Hamilton Heights:
* Hamilton Grange Station Post Office – 521 West 146th Street
* College Station Post Office - 217 West 140th Street
* Fort Washington Post Office – 556 West 158th Street<ref>{{cite web | title=PO Locator - USPS | website=USPS.com | url=https://tools.usps.com/find-location.htm?locationType=po&address=10031&searchRadius=20&fdbid=1366034& | access-date=March 18, 2020}}</ref>

== Education ==
[[File:OHNY City College of New York - Solar Roofpod and Harlem Garden for Urban Food 2.jpg|thumb|left|View of the City College campus lawn ]]
Community District 9 had a higher rate of college-educated residents than the rest of the city {{as of|2018|lc=y}}. A plurality of residents age 25 and older (49%) had a college education or higher, while 21% had less than a high school education and 30% were high school graduates or had some college education. By contrast, 64% of Manhattan residents and 43% of city residents have a college education or higher.<ref name="CHP2018" />{{Rp|6}} The percentage of students in Community District 9 excelling in math rose from 25% in 2000 to 49% in 2011, and reading achievement increased from 32% to 35% during the same time period.<ref name=":17">{{Cite web|url=http://furmancenter.org/files/sotc/MN_09_11.pdf|title=Morningside Heights/Hamilton – MN 06|date=2011|publisher=[[Furman Center for Real Estate and Urban Policy]]|access-date=October 5, 2016}}</ref>

Community District 9's rate of elementary school student absenteeism is higher than the rest of New York City. In the 2016–17 school year, 27% of elementary school students missed 20 or more days per [[school year]], more than the citywide average of 20%.<ref name=":21" />{{Rp|24 (PDF p. 55)}}<ref name="CHP2018" />{{Rp|6}} Additionally, 65% of high school students in Community District 9 graduate on time, less than the citywide average of 75%.<ref name="CHP2018" />{{Rp|6}}

===Library===
[[File:NYPL Hamilton Grange jeh.JPG|thumb|180px|[[New York Public Library Hamilton Grange Branch|NYPL Hamilton Grange Branch]]]]
The [[New York Public Library]] (NYPL) operates the [[New York Public Library Hamilton Grange Branch|Hamilton Grange branch]] at 503 West 145th Street. It is named after [[Founding Fathers of the United States|"founding father"]] [[Alexander Hamilton]], who lived at [[Hamilton Grange National Memorial|Hamilton Grange]]. The branch, a [[Carnegie library]], opened in 1907 and was renovated in 1975; it is listed on the [[National Register of Historic Places]].<ref>{{cite web | title=About the Hamilton Grange Library | website=The New York Public Library | url=https://www.nypl.org/about/locations/hamilton-grange | access-date=March 23, 2019}}</ref>

==Transportation==
[[File:137th Street–City College IRT Broadway 1053.JPG|thumb|left|300x300px|The [[137th Street–City College station]]]]
The [[New York City Subway]]'s [[IRT Broadway–Seventh Avenue Line]] stops in Hamilton Heights at the [[137th Street–City College (IRT Broadway–Seventh Avenue Line)|137th Street–City College]] and [[145th Street (IRT Broadway–Seventh Avenue Line)|145th Street]] stations ({{NYCS trains|Broadway-Seventh north}}). The [[IND Eighth Avenue Line]] runs under [[St. Nicholas Avenue (Manhattan)|St. Nicholas Avenue]], providing service at [[135th Street (IND Eighth Avenue Line)|135th Street]] ({{NYCS trains|Eighth center local}}), [[145th Street (IND Eighth Avenue Line)|145th Street]] ({{NYCS trains|Eighth center}}) and [[155th Street (IND Eighth Avenue Line)|155th Street]] ({{NYCS trains|Eighth north local}}). The [[IND Concourse Line]] branches off north of the 145th Street station, and runs under Saint Nicholas Place to serve [[155th Street (IND Concourse Line)|155th Street]] ({{NYCS trains|Concourse local}}).<ref>{{NYCS const|map}}</ref>

The [[MTA Regional Bus Operations]]' {{NYC bus link|M3|M4|M5|M10|M11|M100|M101|Bx6|Bx6 SBS|Bx19|Bx33|prose=y}} buses serve the area.<ref>{{cite NYC bus map|M}}</ref>
